rv.q: But lean into its pagan excess and heart-on-sleeve emoting, and this is a gripping evening.
I’m glad I’ve seen Martin Guerre — but, definitive or not, I found it intriguing rather than devastating, skilful more than soulful.
What you’re left with is Leeds Mis, as a friend quipped.
Indeed, it plays out like a pacy, screamy folk-horror, but one that takes itself far too seriously.
But it is, simply, not a great musical.
You betcha, without the tiniest soupçons of a doubt.
This trimmed-down revival makes a compelling case for a long-misunderstood work.

There is a thrill to it as fingers point and tempers boil, but without breathing room for its characters, emotions are crammed down our throats. Though only Bertrande achieves three dimensionality, an impassionate Liv Andrusier 's performance is the production's anchor, but others are not so lucky.
And yet, it still doesn’t quite earn its place among the golden greats.
The whole cast is fantastic; their voices are nothing short of angelic, and watching the play in the round really brings it all so very close.

Following Les Misérables and Miss Saigon, Martin Guerre was always the problem-child show for Boublil and Schönberg. First staged to mixed critical reactions in London in 1996, it is understandable that, much like their protagonist, the duo wanted to return after a long absence to try to fix this problematic folk tale.
It's not that Martin Guerre is bad at all, it just struggles to work out that final step from goodness to greatness.
This is an accomplished and beautifully performed production, but for me, Martin Guerre deserves to be a little more epic.
It is gripping in its own way, but it is neither epic, nor does it quite have the intimacy of a love story.

cn.t: Boublil and Schönberg's oft-revised musical receives mixed reviews in its "definitive" Old Vic production. Critics praise the ensemble vocals and staging but question whether it reaches the emotional heights of Les Mis and Miss Saigon.
